intuition: A permutation puts all the numbers in an order. Build that order one position at a time by choosing any number not already used. After exploring a choice, remove it so another choice can use that position. Save a copy when the order contains every number.

The current path is the unfinished permutation; used answers whether a value is already in it. Choose any unused value, append it, and recursively fill the next position. When the path reaches input length, all positions are assigned and every value is used once. Save a copy because the original path is about to change.

Returning from recursion does not automatically undo list or set mutations. Remove the just-added value from both path and used before trying a sibling branch. This restoration is what makes the search tree systematic: siblings share the same prefix but choose different next values.
Every full permutation corresponds to one unique root-to-leaf sequence of choices, so no duplicates or omissions occur.

There are n! distinct answers: the first position has n choices, the next n-1, and so on. Each answer contains n values, so merely returning all answers requires O(n·n!) storage and time. The O(n) additional-space claim counts only the current path, used set, and recursion frames; it excludes the returned lists.
At the maximum n=6, there are 720 answers, which makes output growth part of the task rather than an inefficiency of backtracking.

steps: For [1,2,3], begin with path=[] and used=set() and choose 1 first.
Choose 2 next, then 3. Copy [1,2,3] into result when the path is full.
Undo 3 and then 2. Choose 3 after prefix [1], then 2, saving [1,3,2].
Undo back to the empty prefix and choose 2 first, producing [2,1,3] and [2,3,1].
Choose 3 first for the final two branches, producing [3,1,2] and [3,2,1].
Return all six saved lists; their outer ordering is not part of the answer requirement.

codeNotes.note: Store an independent answer; storing path itself would leave results sharing a repeatedly mutated list.
Reject repeated values before descending, so every explored prefix can still become a permutation.
Undo both state changes so the next sibling branch starts from exactly the same prefix.

keyDecision: A position may use only an unused input number. Undo both the choice and its used marker afterward.

concept.question: What if every unused number could fill the next empty seat?
intuition: A complete ordering cannot reuse a number or leave one out. Generating arbitrary sequences and rejecting duplicates at the end wastes routes that were impossible as soon as a repeated choice appeared.

Build an ordering one seat at a time. At each seat, any unused number can be chosen. After exploring its continuations, release that choice so another branch can occupy the same seat. A full seating arrangement is one permutation.
concept.observation: Each number occupies exactly one seat in a completed ordering.
approach: Choose any unused number for the next position.
Explore its continuations, then release it before the next alternative.
Save an independent copy when all positions are filled.
concept.correctness: The unused-number rule ensures every completed route contains each input number exactly once. Every possible ordering gives a legal next choice at every seat, so its route is explored. Different routes first differ at some seat and therefore produce different permutations. Saving an independent result preserves it when later choices are undone.

complexity.explanation: There are factorially many orderings, and writing each takes linear time in its length. Search bookmarks and the current path use linear auxiliary memory; storing the output dominates for large inputs.

pitfalls: Never reuse a number within one ordering.
Undo a branch before trying another.
Save copies rather than references to the changing path.
